turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell was appalled, she thought, by the lack of propriety and good breeding exhibited by this...this young man, and she was determined to expose him for the cad he undoubtedly was.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He was afraid he might not be able to tell Lady Bracknell the exact number of his house, but he would try to remember it was a large, old-fashioned house with a great many rooms, and it was in a very respectable part of town.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell was shocked, she declared, by the lack of precision and attention to detail displayed by this young man.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He was afraid he might be getting a bit mixed up, and, well, he didn't want to make a mistake, so perhaps it would be better to ask Mr. Worthing for the exact number, if Lady Bracknell would be so kind as to excuse him for just a moment.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Good heavens, Jack, Lady Bracknell was appalled, this was not a habit of his, to be so vague and uncertain about even the simplest of things.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He was worried that Lady Bracknell might think him a bit unsuitable, but he was sure that, with a little explanation, she would see that he was quite a respectable young man.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Good heavens, Jack, this is quite unacceptable, a gentleman should know his own address without having to ask for it.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He hoped Lady Bracknell would see that he was trying his best, and that a small mistake didn't necessarily mean he was a completely unreliable person.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Good heavens, Jack, if he is not even certain of his own name, how can he possibly expect to provide for her daughter?

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen was appalled by the absurdity of being treated like a common job applicant, subject to judgment and scrutiny.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He was beginning to feel a bit overwhelmed, to be honest, and he hoped Lady Bracknell wouldn't think him too foolish.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Good heavens, Jack, this is quite unacceptable, a gentleman should know his own family connections without having to ask for them.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Good heavens, Lady Bracknell was interrogating Jack like a common suspect, Gwendolen thought, can't she see he's perfectly capable of taking care of her?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He wished Lady Bracknell would consider that he was trying his best to provide for Gwendolen, despite being a bit rough around the edges.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's eyes narrowed as she surveyed Jack, her voice dripping with disdain. A gentleman, indeed! It was quite clear that he was not a gentleman at all, but rather a cad who had been living a life of unmitigated scandal.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen's eyes flashed with annoyance as she spoke, her voice laced with a hint of indignation. Good heavens, she thought, must Mother be so dreadfully hard on Jack? He's perfectly capable of taking care of me, and she wouldn't be lectured to like a naughty child!

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Good heavens, Jack, Lady Bracknell was taken aback by his vagueness, she thought, a gentleman must be able to provide accurate information about his lineage, without having to think about it for a moment.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He hoped Lady Bracknell would not think him a complete fool, but he was afraid he couldn't tell her exactly where he was born, it was all a bit of a muddle.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's eyes narrowed as she regarded Jack, her voice dripping with disapproval. The fact that he could not recall his place of birth was a serious failing in a gentleman, and a matter of considerable concern to her, particularly since her daughter's future was at stake.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He wished Lady Bracknell would consider the circumstances, it being rather difficult to recall every detail of one's childhood, and, besides, he thought he was quite capable of making a decent husband for Gwendolen.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen told Lady Bracknell that she was engaged to Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Gwendolen and Mr. Worthing to pardon her, as they were not engaged to anyone. She explained that when they did become engaged, she or Mr. Worthing's father, if his health permitted, would inform them of the fact. An engagement should come as a surprise to a young girl, and it was hardly a matter she could arrange for herself. While she was making inquiries, Gwendolen would wait for her below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen called out to Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Gwendolen to wait for her in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen replied to Lady Bracknell that she would wait for her.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Mr. Worthing to take a seat.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack stood tall, his eyes locked on Lady Bracknell, and said that he preferred to remain standing, rather than take a seat.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell informed Mr. Worthing that he was not on her list of eligible young men, although she had the same list as the Duchess of Bolton. However, she was willing to enter his name if his answers were satisfactory. She asked him if he smoked.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing admitted to Lady Bracknell that he smoked.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell was pleased to hear that Mr. Worthing smoked. She believed that a man should have an occupation. There were too many idle men in London. She asked Mr. Worthing how old he was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he was twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell thought that twenty-nine was a good age to get married. She believed that a man who wanted to get married should know either everything or nothing. She asked Mr. Worthing which category he fell into.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing replied to Lady Bracknell that he knew nothing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell was pleased to hear that Mr. Worthing knew nothing. She believed that ignorance was a delicate and exotic fruit that should not be tampered with. She stated that education was unsound and produced no effect in England. If it did, it would be a danger to the upper classes. She asked Mr. Worthing about his income.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that his income was between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing if his income came from land or investments.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing replied to Lady Bracknell that his income came from investments.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell thought that Mr. Worthing's income was satisfactory. She stated that land was no longer a profit or pleasure, but rather a means of gaining position and losing it. She asked Mr. Worthing about his country house.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he had a country house with some land, but he did not depend on it for his income. In fact, the poachers were the only ones who made anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing how many bedrooms his country house had. She also asked if he had a town house, as a girl like Gwendolen could not be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he owned a house in Belgrave Square, but it was let by the year to Lady Bloxham.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing who Lady Bloxham was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack observed that Lady Bracknell went out very little, and that she was a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing what number his house in Belgrave Square was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that his house was number 149.
